analysis.one_liner: Bans bypassing digital locks on copyrighted works and shields internet providers from liability for users' copying.
analysis.headline: Passed the House by voice vote and the Senate by unanimous consent, and was signed into law on October 28, 1998 as Public Law 105-304.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill carried out two 1996 international copyright treaties and then went further. It made it a civil and criminal violation to break the technological locks (digital rights management) that copyright owners put on movies, music, software, and e-books, and to build or sell tools that break those locks. It also gave internet service providers and websites broad protection from copyright lawsuits over what their users do, as long as they remove material when a copyright owner sends a formal notice. It added a statutory license for internet radio royalties, allowed libraries to make three preservation copies instead of one, exempted routine computer repair copying, and created a new ten-year design right for boat hulls.
analysis.who_benefits: Copyright owners — movie studios, record labels, publishers, and software companies — gain a new federal enforcement regime: breaking a digital lock is itself illegal, with statutory damages of $200 to $2,500 per act and criminal penalties up to $500,000 and five years in prison for commercial violations. Internet service providers and websites gain a near-shield from copyright liability for their users' actions if they follow the notice-and-removal process. Internet radio services gain a statutory license to stream recordings, and boat hull designers gain a new ten-year design right.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Movie studios, record labels, and internet providers

how_it_helps.text: Copyright owners can sue anyone who circumvents a technological measure controlling access to a work, and anyone who manufactures or traffics in circumvention tools, with statutory damages of $200-$2,500 per violation and up to triple damages for repeat violations.
Willful commercial violations carry criminal penalties of up to $500,000 or five years in prison for a first offense, and up to $1 million or ten years for repeat offenses.

Internet service providers are shielded from money damages for their users' copyright infringement across four activities — transmitting, caching, storing user material, and linking — provided they remove material expeditiously upon a compliant notice.

Webcasters gain a statutory license to perform sound recordings digitally, setting a royalty pathway for internet radio; owners of original vessel hull designs gain a ten-year protection with registration, seizure, and forfeiture remedies.

Computer owners and repair shops can copy a boot program during maintenance or repair without infringement, and libraries and archives may make three copies for preservation, security, or replacement instead of one.

analysis.who_pays: People who use digital media. Bypassing a digital lock on something you lawfully own is banned by default, no matter what you do afterward; fair use survives on paper, but getting an exemption requires prevailing in a Librarian of Congress rulemaking held every three years. Nonprofit libraries get only a narrow exemption to evaluate purchases, and cannot lend digital copies outside their premises. Security and encryption researchers can circumvent only under tightly conditioned exemptions. Service providers must take down material on a copyright owner's notice, which means accused users lose access first and contest later. Anyone selling circumvention tools faces statutory damages and criminal exposure.

drawbacks.text: The circumvention ban applies to breaking the lock, not just to infringing the work — and the law's own savings clause preserves fair use as a defense to infringement while the separate prohibition on circumvention stands independently, so lawful uses often require an exemption granted by the Librarian of Congress in a proceeding held every three years.

Exemptions are narrow: nonprofit libraries may circumvent only to decide whether to acquire a work, reverse engineering is allowed only for software interoperability, and encryption research and security testing are permitted only under multi-part good-faith conditions, subject to case-by-case factors.

Service providers lose protection unless they remove material expeditiously after a notice, and a provider is shielded for a good-faith removal 'regardless of whether the material or activity is ultimately determined to be infringing' — the burden of contesting falls on the person whose material was taken down, through a counter-notice process.

Analog video recorders must honor automatic gain control and colorstripe copy-control signals, limiting what consumers can legally tape, and copyright owners are barred from applying those technologies only to copying the law still allows.

Statutory damages of $200-$2,500 per act of circumvention and criminal exposure for 'private financial gain' reach well beyond commercial pirates, chilling researchers, hobbyists, and journalists who publish circumvention methods.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill had genuine public benefits: the service-provider safe harbor is a large part of why user-generated platforms and the open web could exist in the United States, and the repair and library provisions solved real problems. But the core of the law — Title I's anti-circumvention regime — shifted the balance of copyright sharply toward rights holders: it makes the act of defeating a digital lock illegal in itself, puts fair use behind a slow, narrow exemption process, and backs it with damages and criminal penalties. The tradeoff was knowingly accepted and, in the House and Senate, never tested by a recorded vote.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it by voice vote under a suspension motion that allows no amendments, the Senate passed its own version by unanimous consent, a conference committee of eight House members and three senators settled the differences in under three weeks, both chambers approved the report without a recorded no vote, and the President signed it on October 28, 1998.

narrative.text: Rep. Howard Coble introduced the bill on July 29, 1997, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which held hearings that September.

The Judiciary Committee reported an amended bill on May 22, 1998, and it was sent sequentially to the Commerce and Ways and Means Committees; Commerce ordered it reported 41-0 on July 17 and reported it July 22, and Ways and Means was discharged the same day.

On August 4, 1998, the House passed the bill by voice vote under suspension of the rules, a fast-track procedure used for noncontroversial bills that requires a two-thirds majority and blocks amendments.

On September 17, 1998, the Senate struck the House text, substituted the language of its own S. 2037 as amended, and passed it by unanimous consent, appointing Senators Hatch, Thurmond, and Leahy as conferees.

The House disagreed to the Senate amendment by unanimous consent on September 23 and appointed conferees including Hyde, Coble, Goodlatte, Conyers, and Berman from Judiciary and Bliley, Tauzin, and Dingell from Commerce; the conference report was filed October 8, agreed to in the Senate by unanimous consent that day, and agreed to in the House by voice vote on October 12.
The President signed the bill on October 28, 1998, and it became Public Law 105-304.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Copyright owners gained the legal backbone for controlling digital access to their works, and internet service providers gained near-immunity from copyright suits over their users' conduct. Consumers and researchers gained only narrow exemptions, and the fight over digital locks shifted to Librarian of Congress rulemakings and the courts rather than Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Movie studios, record labels, and ISPs

for.name: Rep. Howard Coble
for.role: Chair, Subcommittee on Courts and Intellectual Property; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, shepherded it through the House, moved to suspend the rules and pass it, and moved to agree to the conference report.

for.name: House Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Held subcommittee hearings, marked the bill up, and reported it amended on May 22, 1998.

for.name: House Commerce Committee
for.role: Sequential committee with jurisdiction over internet provisions
for.what_they_did: Marked up the bill and ordered it reported by a vote of 41-0 on July 17, 1998, reporting it amended on July 22.

for.name: Sen. Orrin Hatch
for.role: Senate conferee; Chairman, Senate Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Named a Senate conferee; the Senate passed the bill by unanimous consent and insisted on its amendment.

for.name: Sen. Patrick Leahy
for.role: Senate conferee; Ranking Member, Senate Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Named a Senate conferee to resolve the House and Senate versions.

for.name: Motion picture, recording, and software copyright industries
for.role: Principal beneficiaries of the WIPO treaty implementation
for.what_they_did: Championed legislation implementing the 1996 WIPO treaties and the anti-circumvention regime, which the bill's House and Senate sponsors carried through both chambers in 14 months.

for.name: President Bill Clinton
for.what_they_did: Signed the bill into law on October 28, 1998 as Public Law 105-304.

against.name: Library, consumer, and civil liberties groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed the ban on circumventing digital locks and its effect on fair use, libraries, and research; they won narrow exemptions for libraries, encryption research, and security testing but no recorded vote was ever taken on their objections.

against.name: Computer scientists and security researchers
against.what_they_did: Warned that banning the publication of circumvention tools would chill security research and free expression; the final bill added narrowly conditioned research exemptions rather than removing the ban.

sides.party_line_note: The record contains no roll-call votes: the House passed the bill and adopted the conference report by voice vote, the Senate acted by unanimous consent, and the 9 cosponsors split 6 Republicans and 3 Democrats, so the partisan shape cannot be measured from the votes.

industries.industry: Motion picture and music copyright owners
industries.note: The law makes defeating the digital locks these industries place on their products a civil violation and a crime for commercial purposes, and mandates copy-control conformity in analog recorders — locking in their control over how lawful buyers access and use content. The webcasting statutory license also converts internet radio into a royalty stream for record labels.

industries.industry: Internet service providers and online platforms
industries.note: Title II shields providers from monetary liability for their users' infringement across transmission, caching, storage, and linking, provided they operate a notice-and-takedown system — making private platforms the standing enforcement channel for copyright online, with takedowns that can remove accused users' material first and questions asked later.

Manufacturers must build automatic gain control and colorstripe copy-control conformance into analog video recorders and camcorders, raising design constraints for consumers' recording choices, while the law does not require devices to respond to any particular technological measure so long as they do not traffic in circumvention.

Their circumvention exemption is limited to a good-faith evaluation of whether to acquire a commercially exploited work, they cannot lend digital preservation copies outside their premises, and their eligibility for the online safe harbor carries conditions — narrowing the traditional library role in the digital environment.
Title V creates a new ten-year sui generis design right for original vessel hull designs, with registration, import seizure, and forfeiture remedies.
